name: Apollo 13
short_status: Aborted Moon landing, April 11-17, 1970: oxygen tank rupture about 200,000 miles out; all three crew returned safely. NASA's "successful failure".
tagline: NASA · United States · Crewed flyby · 1970 · The space race Partial
stats: farthest humans have ever been from Earth, a record held for 56 years (1970-2026)
cabin temperature at its coldest on the ride home
three men kept alive in a lunar module rated for two men, two days

facts.label: Crew
facts.value: Jim Lovell (commander), Jack Swigert (command module pilot), Fred Haise (lunar module pilot); CM Odyssey, LM Aquarius

facts.label: Late crew swap
facts.value: Swigert replaced Ken Mattingly, announced 10 April 1970, the day before launch, after L-5 blood tests showed Mattingly had no immunity to German measles following exposure via backup crewman Charlie Duke

facts.label: Launch
facts.value: 11 April 1970, 2:13 p.m. EST, Kennedy Space Center Pad 39A, Saturn V SA-508

facts.label: Launch anomaly
facts.value: The S-II center engine shut down about two minutes early; the remaining engines and the S-IVB burned longer to compensate

facts.label: The accident
facts.value: Oxygen tank 2 (serial 10024X-TA0009) ruptured after a routine tank stir at about 55 hours 55 minutes into flight, 9:08 p.m. CST on 13 April 1970, roughly 200,000 miles from Earth; tank 1 failed as a consequence, taking down the CM's power and oxygen

facts.label: First words
facts.value: Swigert: "Okay, Houston, we've had a problem here." Lovell followed with the detail: "We've had a Main B Bus Undervolt."

facts.label: Lifeboat
facts.value: LM Aquarius, designed to support two men for two days, kept three men alive for four; a 34-second burn at 61:30 GET restored the free-return trajectory, raising the closest lunar approach from 69 to 156 miles

facts.label: Farthest point
facts.value: 248,655 miles (400,171 km) from Earth while rounding the lunar far side, 14-15 April 1970; the human distance record until Artemis II reached about 252,756 miles on 6 April 2026

facts.label: S-IVB impact
facts.value: The spent Saturn third stage struck the Moon at GET 77:56:39.7, about 01:09:40 UT on 15 April 1970 (still April 14 in US time zones, the date LROC pages use), at 2.55 S, 27.88 W, north of Mare Cognitum, leaving a roughly 30-meter crater; the Apollo 12 seismometer 135 km away recorded the planned impact

facts.label: PC+2 burn
facts.value: About two hours past the far side, a five-minute burn of Aquarius's descent engine cut the trip home to about 142 hours total mission time

facts.label: CO2 fix
facts.value: Mission Control devised the "mailbox", an adapter of plastic bags, cardboard and tape that fit Odyssey's square lithium hydroxide canisters to Aquarius's round scrubber openings

facts.label: Hardship
facts.value: Cabin temperature fell to 38 degrees Fahrenheit; water was rationed to six ounces per man per day; the crew lost 31.5 pounds combined (Lovell 14); Haise developed a urinary tract infection

facts.label: Splashdown
facts.value: 17 April 1970, Pacific Ocean near Samoa, about one mile from target and four miles from the recovery ship USS Iwo Jima, at mission elapsed time 142:54:41

facts.label: Investigation
facts.value: The Cortright Review Board report (released 15 June 1970) traced a chain: tank dropped about two inches in 1968, thermostat switches welded shut by 65-volt ground power during a 25 March 1970 test that let the heater reach about 1,000 F and damage Teflon wire insulation, then an in-flight stir short-circuit sparked combustion

timeline: Swigert formally replaces Mattingly at a press conference the day before liftoff, after the German measles scare
Liftoff from KSC Pad 39A at 2:13 p.m. EST; the S-II center engine shuts down about two minutes early
9:08 p.m. CST, about 56 hours into flight: oxygen tank 2 ruptures roughly 200,000 miles from Earth. "Okay, Houston, we've had a problem here."
The crew powers up Aquarius as a lifeboat; a 34-second burn at 61:30 GET puts the ship back on a free-return trajectory around the Moon
The discarded S-IVB third stage impacts the Moon at 2.55 S, 27.88 W as planned, about 01:09 UT (April 14 in US time zones); Apollo 12's seismometer 135 km away records it
Rounding the far side, the crew reaches 248,655 miles (400,171 km) from Earth, the farthest humans had ever been
Two hours past the Moon, the five-minute PC+2 burn on Aquarius's descent engine speeds the return home
Service module jettison reveals a whole panel blown away; Aquarius is released ("Farewell, Aquarius, and we thank you"); splashdown near Samoa at 142:54:41, crew safe aboard USS Iwo Jima
Cortright Review Board report released: "an unusual combination of mistakes coupled with a somewhat deficient and unforgiving design"
Artemis II's crew passes Apollo 13's distance record at 12:56 p.m. CDT, peaking near 252,756 miles from Earth
